title: The Order of Events: Lamport from Brooklyn to the Part-Time Parliament
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Brooklyn, birth to two immigrations
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Wikipedia's Early life section places the birth in Brooklyn, and this borough pin replaces the Lower Manhattan coordinate (40.7128, -74.006) carried by one lens of the research pool.
stops.campa: A son is born in Brooklyn to Benjamin Lamport, who came out of Volkovysk in the Russian Empire, and to Hannah Lasser, whose family came from the Austro-Hungarian lands. Both parents are immigrants and the household is Jewish, first generation on both sides. The century he arrives in will spend its second half building machines that cannot see one another and must somehow agree, and no vocabulary for that problem exists yet. They name him Leslie Barry. Nothing else about the day is recorded, not the hospital and not the street.
suggested_refs: Wikipedia, 'Leslie Lamport,' Early life section, on the parents' origins in Volkovysk and the Austro-Hungarian Empire

stops.name: Bronx High School of Science, the exam school
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed. Wikipedia records only that he is a graduate and gives no years at all. The research pool's 'c. 1955-1958' is impossible against his 1960 MIT degree, which requires matriculation around 1956; roughly 1952 to 1956 is the only range that fits, and the month and day here are conventional.
stops.campa: He is admitted to the Bronx High School of Science, a selective public school in the north of the city, built to make scientists out of the children of immigrants and counting Nobel laureates among its later graduates. Whether he touches a computer there, or is taught by anyone whose name survives, is not in the record: no course list, no report card, nothing. He rides the subway up from Brooklyn in the morning and back down at night, four years of it. The building stands at 75 West 205th Street.
suggested_refs: The Bronx High School of Science at 75 West 205th Street, alumni records for the early 1950s

stops.name: MIT, a bachelor's in mathematics
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by Wikipedia; the month is a placement at commencement. The pin is the atlas's canonical MIT campus coordinate, inherited byte-identical from ron_rivest.journey.json rather than the pool's 42.3601, -71.0942.
stops.campa: He takes his degree in mathematics, four years after leaving the Bronx. Computing at MIT in these years is carried on inside other departments by a minority of students and staff, and computer science does not exist as a thing a student can major in: no such faculty, no such degree, no such word to put on a diploma. Lamport is trained as a pure mathematician and will go on calling himself one for decades, long after the field he helps to found has departments and journals of its own. The diploma reads bachelor of science in mathematics, 1960.
suggested_refs: MIT Department of Mathematics commencement records, class of 1960

stops.name: The Mitre Corporation, part-time work at Bedford
stops.date_confidence: attested to the span 1962 to 1965 by Lamport's own account; the month is a placement. The Bedford site is a reconstruction, since the sources name the employer without naming an office and Mitre also ran a Washington-area operation. Two lenses of the research pool omit this employment entirely and begin his working life in 1970.
stops.campa: Two years into graduate work at Brandeis, Lamport takes part-time work at Mitre, the nonprofit corporation set up to run systems engineering for the American military. It is his first paid contact with computers and he is twenty-one when he starts. He gives the years himself as 1962 to 1965 and says almost nothing more about them: no paper comes out of the period, and what he worked on there is in no reachable record. The mathematics and the day job run side by side for three years.
suggested_refs: Lamport's own career summaries, the only source naming the Mitre years
sources: Lamport's own account of his employment, 1962-1965

stops.name: Brandeis University, the master's in mathematics
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the month is a placement at commencement.
stops.campa: The master's in pure mathematics is awarded at Waltham, and he stays on toward a doctorate under Richard Palais, a geometer working in global analysis. The subject is differential equations, not machines. He will not finish the doctorate for another nine years, and the reason is not the mathematics: from here on he is employed, first part time and then not. Whether he meant to let it wait that long, or simply took the work in front of him, no source reached here says.
suggested_refs: Brandeis University mathematics department records for Richard Palais's students, 1960s

stops.name: Marlboro College, teaching mathematics in Vermont
stops.date_confidence: attested to the span 1965 to 1969 by Lamport's own account; the month is a placement at the start of an academic year, and the coordinate is the college's Potash Hill campus rather than any named building.
stops.campa: He leaves Mitre for a teaching post at Marlboro College, a very small liberal arts college on a hill in southern Vermont, and spends four years there teaching mathematics to undergraduates. The dissertation is still unfinished, and Waltham is now a long drive away. Nothing on this hill anticipates the rest of the life: no laboratory, no machines to speak of, no colleague working on concurrency, no reason to think about clocks. He is twenty-four when he arrives and twenty-eight when he leaves. For those four years the technical record is blank.
suggested_refs: Marlboro College faculty records for the mathematics department, 1965-1969
sources: Lamport's own account of his employment, 1965-1969

stops.name: Brandeis University, the doctorate at thirty-one
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the month is not recorded in any source reached here and defaults to January.
stops.campa: Brandeis awards the degree for a dissertation called The Analytic Cauchy Problem with Singular Data, on singularities in solutions to partial differential equations, supervised by Richard Palais. It has nothing to do with computers and he never publishes in the field again. Nine years stand between the master's and this page, filled by a defense contractor and a Vermont classroom, and by the time the degree is conferred he has been working in the computer industry for two years already. He is thirty-one.
suggested_refs: Leslie Lamport, 'The Analytic Cauchy Problem with Singular Data,' Ph.D. dissertation, Brandeis University, 1972

stops.name: Massachusetts Computer Associates, the office park at Wakefield
stops.date_confidence: attested to the span 1970 to 1977; the month is not recorded and defaults to January. The Wakefield address, Lakeside Office Park, comes from the author's-address footnote of his own 1974 CACM paper, read from the PDF.
stops.campa: He joins a small software firm in an office park north of Boston and stays seven years. He becomes a computer scientist here, in a contractor's office, writing software for other people's problems, and in the margins of that beginning a lifetime's work on how independent processes can share anything at all without a referee standing over them. No university laboratory is involved and no famous industrial lab. The firm leaves almost no public trace apart from the address printed at the foot of his papers: Lakeside Office Park, Wakefield, Massachusetts.
suggested_refs: Lakeside Office Park, Wakefield, Massachusetts, the address given in Lamport's 1974 CACM paper

stops.name: Wakefield, the bakery algorithm
stops.date_confidence: attested to the issue: Communications of the ACM 17(8), August 1974, pp. 453-455, read from the paper PDF; no day applies. One lens of the research pool tagged this [R], gave it no date, and placed it at SRI in Menlo Park, which the paper's own byline and address footnote refute, since he did not join SRI until 1977.
stops.campa: Under the title A New Solution of Dijkstra's Concurrent Programming Problem, Lamport publishes the algorithm everyone will call the bakery. Each process takes a number on arrival, as at a bakery counter, and the lowest number goes first. It needs no atomic instruction from the hardware, only memory that can be read and written, and it keeps working even when a read overlaps a write and comes back with nonsense. The byline reads Massachusetts Computer Associates, Inc., Wakefield.
stops.quote: I have invented many concurrent algorithms. I feel that I did not invent the bakery algorithm, I discovered it.
stops.quote_source: Leslie Lamport, annotated publications page, entry on the bakery algorithm, lamport.azurewebsites.net/pubs/pubs.html
suggested_refs: Leslie Lamport, 'A New Solution of Dijkstra's Concurrent Programming Problem,' CACM 17(8), August 1974
sources: Lamport's annotated publications page, raw HTML

stops.name: Wakefield, the last winter in Massachusetts
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of the move; the month is a placement, and no source reached here gives a date for his departure from the firm.
stops.campa: Seven years at the firm end. He is thirty-six, holds a mathematics doctorate awarded five years earlier, and has published on how processes that share nothing but memory can take turns without colliding. The next problem is the same problem with the memory taken away: processes that share nothing but messages, and messages that arrive late, or in the wrong order, or never. He will not work in Massachusetts again. The move west is three thousand miles and he makes it in 1977.
suggested_refs: Massachusetts Computer Associates, Inc., corporate records for the 1970s

stops.name: SRI International, arriving on Ravenswood Avenue
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the month is a placement. The pin is the atlas's canonical SRI coordinate, inherited byte-identical from bob_kahn.journey.json and vint_cerf.journey.json; one lens of the research pool pinned SRI at 37.4419, -122.143, which is downtown Palo Alto and about 3.5 km wrong.
stops.campa: He joins SRI International at Menlo Park, a research contractor cut loose from Stanford a few years earlier and living on defense and aerospace money. The second node of the ARPANET has been running on this campus since 1969, and the place is thick with people whose machines must talk to other machines over links that fail. Lamport is hired into the computer science laboratory at 333 Ravenswood Avenue. What he was hired specifically to do is recorded nowhere reached here. Within a year he is working on SIFT.
suggested_refs: SRI International, 333 Ravenswood Avenue, Menlo Park, computer science laboratory in the late 1970s

stops.name: SRI International, the SIFT project
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the project and his participation, which the sources date to a period of roughly 1977 to 1980 rather than to an event; the year and month here are a placement inside that span.
stops.campa: SIFT, Software Implemented Fault Tolerance, is a NASA contract to build an aircraft flight-control computer out of ordinary processors that vote on every result, so that a machine which has gone wrong can be outvoted instead of trusted. The voting is not the hard part. A broken processor need not fail silently: it can send one answer to one neighbor and a contradictory answer to another, and behave, from outside, exactly like a liar. The engineers on the project name this difficulty before Lamport ever arrives.
stops.quote: I am often unfairly credited with inventing the Byzantine agreement problem. The problem was formulated by people working on SIFT before I arrived at SRI.
stops.quote_source: Leslie Lamport, annotated publications page, entry on 'Reaching Agreement in the Presence of Faults,' lamport.azurewebsites.net/pubs/pubs.html
suggested_refs: The SIFT fault-tolerant flight control computer, NASA contract reports from SRI International
sources: Lamport's annotated publications page, raw HTML, anchor '#reaching'

stops.name: SRI International, Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events
stops.date_confidence: attested to the issue: Communications of the ACM 21(7), July 1978, pp. 558-565, read from the paper PDF; no day applies.
stops.campa: The paper is seven pages long and it begins by taking the clock away. If two events happen in different processes and no message passes between them, there is no fact of the matter about which came first. So Lamport builds an ordering out of what a system can actually know: one event precedes another if they are in the same process in that order, or if the first is the sending of a message and the second its receipt, or by chaining those two rules together. Out of that comes a counter each process keeps alone, and a single order the whole system can agree on with no shared second hand anywhere in it.
stops.quote: In a distributed system, it is sometimes impossible to say that one of two events occurred first. The relation "happened before" is therefore only a partial ordering of the events in the system.
stops.quote_source: Leslie Lamport, 'Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System,' Communications of the ACM 21, no. 7 (July 1978), p. 558
suggested_refs: Leslie Lamport, 'Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System,' CACM 21(7), July 1978, pp. 558-565

stops.name: SRI International, Reaching Agreement in the Presence of Faults
stops.date_confidence: attested to the issue: Journal of the ACM 27(2), April 1980, pp. 228-234. The byline order is Pease, Shostak, Lamport, correcting one lens of the research pool, which wrote 'With Marshall Pease and Robert Shostak, Lamport publishes.' The same lens garbled the bound as '3n+1', reusing n for both the total and the faulty count; the result is n >= 3m+1, and the campa states it in words to avoid re-importing the error.
stops.campa: Marshall Pease, Robert Shostak, and Lamport publish the result underneath SIFT. To survive some number of components that may lie in arbitrary and mutually inconsistent ways, a system needs more than three times that number in total. Three processors cannot outlast one traitor among them. Four can. The proof concerns what is knowable from messages alone, and it lays a hard floor under every later scheme for making unreliable machines behave as one reliable machine. Lamport's name is third on the paper.
suggested_refs: Pease, Shostak and Lamport, 'Reaching Agreement in the Presence of Faults,' JACM 27(2), April 1980, pp. 228-234

stops.name: SRI International, the Byzantine generals
stops.date_confidence: attested to the issue: ACM Transactions on Programming Languages and Systems 4(3), July 1982, pp. 382-401, read from the paper PDF. The byline here is Lamport, Shostak, Pease, which is a different order from the 1980 JACM paper and a third order again from the one the research pool's chronology lens gives.
stops.campa: Two years later the same theorem comes back in costume. Divisions of an army camp around a city, each under its own general, and they can communicate only by messenger; some of the generals are traitors who will tell one colleague to attack and another to retreat. The mathematics is unchanged from 1980. The picture is what travels. Engineers who will never open the paper say Byzantine fault forty years later, and most of them could not name the three authors or the year.
stops.quote: We imagine that several divisions of the Byzantine army are camped outside an enemy city, each division commanded by its own general. The generals can communicate with one another only by messenger.
stops.quote_source: Lamport, Shostak and Pease, 'The Byzantine Generals Problem,' ACM Transactions on Programming Languages and Systems 4, no. 3 (July 1982), pp. 382-383
suggested_refs: Lamport, Shostak and Pease, 'The Byzantine Generals Problem,' ACM TOPLAS 4(3), July 1982

stops.name: Stanford University, Knuth's typesetting engine
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed. The sources place Lamport's adoption of TeX in the early 1980s without giving a date, and this year is a placement inside that period; Donald Knuth began TeX at Stanford in 1977-78. The pin is the atlas's canonical Stanford coordinate, inherited byte-identical.
stops.campa: A few miles from Menlo Park, Donald Knuth has spent years building TeX, a typesetting system meant to give an author, and above all a mathematician, control over every mark on the printed page. Lamport wants to write a book about concurrency and takes up TeX to set it. He finds the thing exact and unforgiving, nearer to a programming language than to a typewriter. So he begins writing macros: a layer between the author and the engine, so that the author can ask for a theorem instead of asking for a font and a vertical skip.
stops.quote: In the early 80s, I was planning to write the Great American Concurrency Book. I was a TeX user, so I would need a set of macros. I thought that, with a little extra effort, I could make my macros usable by others. Don Knuth had begun issuing early releases of the current version of TeX, and I figured I could write what would become its standard macro package. That was the beginning of LaTeX.
stops.quote_source: Leslie Lamport, annotated publications page, entry on 'LaTeX: A Document Preparation System,' lamport.azurewebsites.net/pubs/pubs.html
suggested_refs: Donald Knuth, The TeXbook, and the early TeX releases issued from Stanford in the late 1970s and early 1980s
sources: Lamport's annotated publications page, raw HTML

stops.name: SRI International, the macros become a system
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed. The sources give 1983 as the period in which the macros were written, with releases following in 1984 and 1985; the month is a placement.
stops.campa: The macro package acquires a name, LaTeX, and a design principle that is not Knuth's. The author declares structure: this is a section, this is a theorem, this is a citation, this is a bibliography. The system decides how any of it looks. It divides the labor between two kinds of expertise, and most working scientists neither have the second kind nor should need it in order to publish an argument about neutrinos. The book it was written to serve is never written.
suggested_refs: The earliest circulating LaTeX macro files, written at SRI International
sources: Lamport's annotated publications page, raw HTML

stops.name: SRI International, LaTeX goes out
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1984 for a release by Wikipedia, which names no version. The string 'LaTeX 2.06a in September 1984' carried by the research pool could not be sourced in this pass, the LaTeX Project's history page returning HTTP 404, so both the version and the month are reconstruction.
stops.campa: The package goes out to other people in 1984. It spreads the way tools spread through a research culture with no marketing and no purchase orders: a tape, a colleague, a departmental machine, a habit. Nobody owns the expectation it creates and there is no committee behind it. Physicists take it up, then mathematicians, then the computer scientists among whom it was written. Within a few years an author submitting a paper in these fields is expected to submit it in LaTeX.
suggested_refs: The 1984 LaTeX release and its distribution through university computing centres

stops.name: Palo Alto, the last version he maintains alone
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1985 for a further release. The version string 'LaTeX 2.09' and the month of August come from the research pool and could not be confirmed in this pass; both are carried as reconstruction.
stops.campa: The last version Lamport maintains by himself goes out in 1985, by which time he is working for Digital Equipment Corporation in Palo Alto and the typesetting is a second job done in the evenings. It will stand as the working standard of physics, mathematics, and computer science for the better part of a decade, on machines in every country that has universities, supported by one man answering his own mail about it. Nobody is paying him for any of this.
suggested_refs: The 1985 LaTeX release, the last issued under Lamport's sole maintenance

stops.name: Palo Alto, the LaTeX book
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of publication by Addison-Wesley; the month is not recorded and defaults to January.
stops.campa: Addison-Wesley publishes LaTeX: A Document Preparation System, a few hundred pages that teach the system to nearly everyone who will ever use it. It sells into the hundreds of thousands, a figure no typesetting manual has any business reaching. For most of a generation of scientists it is the only documentation they ever open, and it is not a book with a title and an author but an object at the edge of a desk, spine broken, splayed open and face down.
suggested_refs: Leslie Lamport, LaTeX: A Document Preparation System (Addison-Wesley, 1986)

stops.name: Stanford University, handing LaTeX away
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: the handoff is dated 21 August 1989, at a TeX Users Group meeting held at Stanford.
stops.campa: At a TeX Users Group meeting he gives the system away. Frank Mittelbach takes over its maintenance and, with Chris Rowley and Rainer Schöpf, forms the team that rebuilds it as LaTeX2e in 1994, the version still in use decades afterward. A successor called LaTeX3 is announced as the next generation and never arrives as one; in 2018 it is folded in as a programming layer inside its own predecessor. Lamport is forty-eight and has been maintaining the thing single-handed for six years.
suggested_refs: The TeX Users Group meeting at Stanford, 21 August 1989, and the formation of the LaTeX3 team

stops.name: DEC Systems Research Center, Lytton Avenue
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of the move; the month is not recorded and defaults to January. One lens of the research pool describes his DEC years as spent at Maynard, Massachusetts, which was DEC's corporate headquarters and not the Systems Research Center; every other source places him in Palo Alto, and the contradiction is recorded in the report.
stops.campa: He leaves SRI for the Systems Research Center, the laboratory Digital Equipment Corporation keeps in downtown Palo Alto, a few streets from the Stanford campus and across town from Xerox PARC. It is one of the last of the great corporate research laboratories of the period, staffed to think rather than to ship, and generous with the years a proof takes. The address is on Lytton Avenue. He is forty-four, and he will work there sixteen years and under two owners.
suggested_refs: The DEC Systems Research Center on Lytton Avenue, Palo Alto, 1985-2001

stops.name: Palo Alto, the parliament of Paxos
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1989 for the submission; the sources date the drafting to 1989 and 1990 and give no month, so the month here is a placement.
stops.campa: He writes a protocol by which a group of unreliable machines can agree on a sequence of decisions, and he writes it as archaeology. On the Aegean island of Paxos, the paper reports, a parliament conducted its business although its legislators wandered in and out of the chamber as their other trades required, and the recovered fragments of its procedure are reconstructed here for the modern reader. Under the invented ethnography sits an algorithm as rigorous as the Byzantine paper. The referees do not know what to do with it, and the manuscript sits.
stops.quote: Early in this millennium, the Aegean island of Paxos was a thriving mercantile center. Wealth led to political sophistication, and the Paxons replaced their ancient theocracy with a parliamentary form of government.
stops.quote_source: Leslie Lamport, 'The Part-Time Parliament,' ACM Transactions on Computer Systems 16, no. 2 (May 1998), p. 134
suggested_refs: The 1989 submission of 'The Part-Time Parliament' to ACM Transactions on Computer Systems

stops.name: Palo Alto, the Temporal Logic of Actions
stops.date_confidence: attested to the period: successive versions of the temporal logic are published in 1990 and 1994. The month is a placement at the start of that span.
stops.campa: Alongside the algorithms he builds a logic. TLA, the Temporal Logic of Actions, is a notation for saying exactly what a concurrent system is supposed to do, in a form precise enough that the saying can be checked before anything is built out of it. The logic grows into TLA+, and TLA+ into a toolchain he will keep refining for thirty years. The proposition underneath does not change in that time: an engineer who cannot write down what a system should do has no way of finding out whether the code does it.
suggested_refs: Lamport's TLA papers of 1990 and 1994, the basis of the later TLA+ language

stops.name: Palo Alto, behind the filing cabinet
stops.date_confidence: attested to the issue: ACM Transactions on Computer Systems 16(2), May 1998, p. 133ff, read from the paper PDF; no day applies.
stops.campa: Nine years after it was submitted, the parliament paper is printed with its Greek ethnography intact and an editorial note in front of it, explaining that the submission had lately been discovered behind a filing cabinet in the editorial office. The joke is kept up on both sides. What the paper describes under the costume becomes the standing answer to how a cluster of machines agrees on anything, and the word Paxos passes into ordinary engineering speech. The issue is Transactions on Computer Systems, volume 16, number 2, May 1998, page 133.
stops.quote: This submission was recently discovered behind a filing cabinet in the TOCS editorial office. Despite its age, the editor-in-chief felt that it was worth publishing.
stops.quote_source: Keith Marzullo, editorial note prefacing Leslie Lamport, 'The Part-Time Parliament,' ACM Transactions on Computer Systems 16, no. 2 (May 1998), p. 133
suggested_refs: Leslie Lamport, 'The Part-Time Parliament,' ACM TOCS 16(2), May 1998, with Marzullo's editorial note

stops.name: Palo Alto, the employer changes its name
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1998 for Compaq's acquisition of Digital Equipment Corporation; the day is not recorded in the research pool and the month is a placement.
stops.campa: Compaq buys Digital Equipment Corporation, and the laboratory on Lytton Avenue gets new letterhead. Lamport's office does not move, his colleagues do not change, his telephone number does not change, and neither does the question he has been working on for twenty years in several disguises: how machines that cannot see one another, and cannot trust one another's clocks, come to agree about anything whatever. He has been thirteen years at this address by now, and will be three more before he leaves it.
suggested_refs: Compaq's 1998 acquisition of Digital Equipment Corporation and the fate of the Systems Research Center

stops.name: Palo Alto, Paxos Made Simple
stops.date_confidence: attested to 2001 for publication in ACM SIGACT News; the month is not recorded and defaults to January.
stops.campa: Readers keep telling him the parliament paper is impenetrable, so he writes it again with the island taken out: no archaeology, no legislators, no invented civilisation, just the algorithm and its proof. He calls the result Paxos Made Simple and publishes it in SIGACT News in 2001. A small literature of further explanations grows up around both versions, written by other people, each promising to be the one that finally makes it plain. Whether the second telling is clearer than the first is still argued in graduate seminars.
suggested_refs: Leslie Lamport, 'Paxos Made Simple,' ACM SIGACT News, 2001

stops.name: Microsoft Research Silicon Valley, La Avenida Street
stops.date_confidence: attested to 2001 for the move; the lab itself opened in August 2001. The coordinate is 1065 La Avenida Street, Mountain View, correcting a research-pool coordinate of 37.4224, -122.1131 that falls in the Palo Alto baylands about 3.5 km away.
stops.campa: Microsoft opens a research laboratory at 1065 La Avenida Street in Mountain View, and Lamport joins it, his fourth industrial employer and his third inside a twelve-mile stretch of the Peninsula. The work from here on is almost entirely formal methods: the specification language, its model checker, the documentation for both. The rest of it is persuasion, carried out on engineers who have never written a specification in their lives and do not, at first, see why they should start. He is sixty years old.
suggested_refs: Microsoft Research Silicon Valley, 1065 La Avenida Street, Mountain View, opened August 2001

stops.name: Mountain View, Specifying Systems
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of publication; the month is not recorded and defaults to January.
stops.campa: The book on TLA+ appears in 2002, subtitled for hardware and software engineers rather than for logicians. The errors the language catches on paper are the kind that otherwise surface in production, years later and under load. Amazon will use it to check the designs of its storage services and Microsoft to check its own. Like the LaTeX manual sixteen years before it, the book becomes the way practitioners learn a notation that one man designed almost single-handed.
suggested_refs: Leslie Lamport, Specifying Systems: The TLA+ Language and Tools for Hardware and Software Engineers (2002)

stops.name: Mountain View, the model checker
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed. The sources describe the extension of TLA+ and its TLC model checker as continuous work across the Mountain View years rather than as a dated event, and the year here is a placement inside that span.
stops.campa: Between flights to European ceremonies he sits in Mountain View extending the toolchain: TLC, the model checker that walks every state a specification can reach, looking for the one that breaks the property its author claimed. The work is unglamorous. Much of it is writing and debugging ordinary code, and he does most of that himself, at sixty-seven, when a man with his citation count would ordinarily be delivering keynotes. The bug reports arrive by mail and he answers them.
suggested_refs: TLC, the TLA+ model checker, and its development at Microsoft Research

stops.name: Portland, the influential paper
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 2000, at the ACM Symposium on Principles of Distributed Computing, held that year in Portland, Oregon; the host city is confirmed by podc.org/podc2000/, which carries a Portland visitor page, so the research pool's [R] hedge is lifted. The award was then the PODC Influential-Paper Award and was renamed the Edsger W. Dijkstra Prize only after 2002; the pool's use of the later name for this year is anachronistic. The month is not recorded.
stops.campa: Twenty-two years after it appeared, the clocks paper is given the field's award for lasting influence, at a conference in Oregon. The prize is called the PODC Influential-Paper Award at this point; it becomes the Edsger W. Dijkstra Prize only after 2002. Lamport takes it twice more, in 2005 for the agreement paper and again in 2014, three times in all. On his own annotated list of publications he records, against this paper, what Jim Gray once told him about it.
stops.quote: Jim Gray once told me that he had heard two different opinions of this paper: that it's trivial and that it's brilliant. I can't argue with the former, and I am disinclined to argue with the latter.
stops.quote_source: Leslie Lamport, annotated publications page, entry on 'Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System,' lamport.azurewebsites.net/pubs/pubs.html
suggested_refs: The PODC Influential-Paper Award of 2000, later renamed the Edsger W. Dijkstra Prize in Distributed Computing
sources: Lamport's annotated publications page, raw HTML

stops.name: Rennes, the first honorary doctorate
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; neither month nor day is recorded in any source reached here, and both default.
stops.campa: The University of Rennes gives him a doctorate honoris causa, the first of five European ones in four years. The theory was written in office parks along a thirty-mile strip of California suburb, by a man with no university appointment at any point in his career, and it is by now taught in every European computer science faculty that teaches concurrency at all. He flies over for the ceremony. Then he flies back and goes on writing the model checker.
suggested_refs: University of Rennes honorary doctorate records, 2003

stops.name: Kiel, the second doctorate of the same year
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the month is not recorded, and the order of the two 2003 doctorates is not recorded either.
stops.campa: Christian-Albrechts-Universität honors him in the same year as Rennes, and no source records which of the two came first. There is no relocation behind any of these degrees and no sabbatical: each is a few days lifted out of a working life spent almost entirely inside a few square miles of the San Francisco Peninsula. The German and the French reception of distributed-systems theory has run a decade ahead of the American one. Kiel is on the Baltic coast; he is in the city for the ceremony and out of it again within days.
suggested_refs: Christian-Albrechts-Universität zu Kiel, honorary doctorate records, 2003

stops.name: Lausanne, the doctorate at EPFL
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the month is not recorded. The IEEE Emanuel R. Piore Award of the same year is likewise attested, but its presentation venue is recorded nowhere reached in this pass, so it is folded into this stop rather than given an invented pin of its own, as the research pool did at 40.7484, -73.9857.
stops.campa: EPFL adds a doctorate on Lake Geneva. Switzerland is thick with verification and formal-methods groups, and the reception in these buildings is not merely ceremonial: people here write specifications in his notation and prove things about them for a living. In the same year IEEE gives him the Emanuel R. Piore Award, which recognises the accumulated weight of the SRI and DEC papers rather than any single result among them. Where that ceremony was held, nobody wrote down.

stops.campa: The Università della Svizzera italiana confers a fourth honorary doctorate at Lugano, in the Italian-speaking canton south of the Alps. He is sixty-five. It is the fourth of five, and the last of them is a year away. Between these trips the shape of the work does not alter at all: specifications, the model checker, and mail from engineers who have found a bug in a tool with perhaps four hundred serious users in the world. He answers that mail himself.

In the same year the clocks paper enters the operating-systems hall of fame, and five years afterward the parliament paper joins it there. Where either induction was presented is not recorded: the odd-year award goes out at one conference and the even-year award at another, and no source reached here names a room for either. stops.campa: He is elected to the National Academy of Sciences, whose building stands on Constitution Avenue among the monuments and the museums. Concurrency theory did not exist as a named discipline when he took his first degree, and neither did the job title. The Academy elects him as a computer scientist. He entered that category sideways at twenty-nine, out of the singularities of partial differential equations, by way of a software contractor in an office park north of Boston.

The prize goes to work whose impact has proved durable. Durability can be measured a simpler way here: engineers use the adjective daily without knowing that there was ever a paper behind it. The conference that year is Dependable Systems and Networks, and the host city is reported as Budapest but not confirmed.

stops.campa: ACM names him the 2013 recipient of the A. M. Turing Award, the highest honor the discipline has, for the theory and practice of distributed and concurrent systems: causality and logical clocks, safety and liveness, replicated state machines, sequential consistency. The citation names concepts rather than a single result, which is unusual for the prize, and each of those concepts entered the field through a paper of his. The oldest of them is thirty-six years old on the day of the announcement.

stops.campa: The award is presented at the annual banquet, thirty-five miles up the peninsula from the office where he works, in front of an industry that has been running his algorithms underneath its products for a generation. In the same year ACM makes him a Fellow and the Dijkstra Prize comes to him for a third time, so that within twelve months he collects nearly everything the field has left to give a living person. He is seventy-three. On the Monday he is back at the model checker, which still has bugs in it.

Most of the staff are let go on a few days' notice, and the laboratory that opened in August 2001 closes for good. He is seventy-three. Lamport stays with Microsoft Research and works on from wherever he happens to be, without the building and without the corridor. He has been thirteen years at La Avenida Street. stops.name: Mountain View, retirement at eighty-three
stops.date_confidence: attested to January 2025; the day is not recorded. The pin marks the institution rather than a room, since the Mountain View building had been closed for a decade and no source reached here says where he was working at the end. The research pool's count of four employers undercounts: Mitre and Marlboro College precede Massachusetts Computer Associates.
stops.campa: He retires from Microsoft Research in January, a few weeks short of his eighty-fourth birthday, having been paid to think about computers since 1962 by Mitre, a college in Vermont, a software firm in Wakefield, SRI, DEC, Compaq, and Microsoft. He is living, so there is no tomb here and no epitaph. What stands instead is textual: papers in every distributed-systems syllabus, consensus protocols running under services half the world touches daily, specifications written in a language he designed alone. A blockchain launched in 2020 calls its smallest unit of currency a lamport.
